# Changelog

## 2026-07-01
- Ran Kaggle 2xT4 Stream1 piece-transformer benchmark version 4 after pushing commit `08d1ddd`. Fresh CUDA tensor-GEMM attention backend completed with best per-T4 rows: GPU0 `401869.4` candidates/s at `B_MICRO=1024, concurrency=1`; GPU1 `411356.9` candidates/s at `B_MICRO=512, concurrency=2`; aggregate `813226.3` candidates/s. This is `~0.55x` of direct PyTorch fast forward and `~0.64-0.65x` of PyTorch `batch_process`, so it is not a hard ceiling. Evidence is recorded in `test_results/stream1_transformer_kaggle_benchmark_v4_2026-07-01.md`.
- Added `kaggle_transformer_inference_speed/`, a private Kaggle script-kernel derived from `vladkuznetsov266/transformer-inference-example` to benchmark the model artifact inference speed directly. Version 2 completed on Tesla T4 with `torch=2.10.0+cu128`, `backend=fast`; best direct forward was `batch=2048`, `734786.8` candidates/s, and searcher-like `batch_process` for `65536` rows with `eval_batch_size=16384` was `630697.0` candidates/s. Evidence is recorded in `test_results/transformer_inference_example_kaggle_speed_2026-07-01.md`.

## 2026-06-30
- Added `tools/stream1_transformer_torch_benchmark.py`, a plain PyTorch fp16 Stream1 piece-transformer inference benchmark over the exported weight files. In local Docker `cmz-native-dev:2026-05-26` on RTX 3070 Laptop GPU, reference validation passed with max score-key error `26`; best eager SDPA point was `batch=2048`, `613885.6` candidates/s, with larger batches dropping sharply. Results are recorded in `test_results/stream1_transformer_torch_benchmark_2026-06-30.md` and `test_results/stream1_transformer_torch_benchmark_large_2026-06-30.md`.
- Optimized Stream1 `piece_transformer` inference hot path after Nsight profiling: removed per-thread `State128` copies in token build, added a `cols==256` LayerNorm fast path, added an<truncated omitted_approx_tokens="1371" />UDA allocations on exceptions. Verification recorded in `test_results/stream1_transformer_loader_2026-06-29.md`.
- Added the Stream1 piece-transformer host loader path and scratch arena scaffolding without wiring transformer inference. The weight loader now parses and validates the exact p900 piece-transformer manifest contract, loads exported transformer tensors and piece layout tables with exact byte sizes, exposes host/device/scratch byte helpers, and keeps MLP loading on an explicit separate branch. Verification recorded in `test_results/stream1_transformer_loader_2026-06-29.md`.
- Added Stream1 piece-transformer export tooling: an auto-detecting tools/export_stream1.py wrapper and tools/export_stream1_transformer.py for Kaggle p900 PilgrimPieceTransformer checkpoints. The exporter writes fast-slot input tables, piece layout tensors, Transformer block tensors, manifests with backend=piece_transformer, rejects non-24-output, non-4-layer, and non-1024-FF variants, and supports optional CPU fp32 reference JSON generation. Verification recorded in test_results/stream1_transformer_exporter_2026-06-29.md.
- Added tagged Stream1 model backend config constants and transformer metadata fields, preserving existing MLP defaults. Stream1 row-mode helpers now force the piece-transformer backend to parent rows while keeping MLP one-output child-row behavior, with contract coverage recorded in `test_results/stream1_piece_transformer_task1_2026-06-29.md`. Unknown Stream1 backend values now fail closed in row-mode helpers, MLP weight validation, and manifest backend parsing; legacy manifests without `backend` still default to MLP.

# Changelog

## 2026-07-01
- Ran Kaggle 2xT4 Stream1 piece-transformer benchmark version 4 after pushing commit `08d1ddd`. Fresh CUDA tensor-GEMM attention backend completed with best per-T4 rows: GPU0 `401869.4` candidates/s at `B_MICRO=1024, concurrency=1`; GPU1 `411356.9` candidates/s at `B_MICRO=512, concurrency=2`; aggregate `813226.3` candidates/s. This is `~0.55x` of direct PyTorch fast forward and `~0.64-0.65x` of PyTorch `batch_process`, so it is not a hard ceiling. Evidence is recorded in `test_results/stream1_transformer_kaggle_benchmark_v4_2026-07-01.md`.
- Added `kaggle_transformer_inference_speed/`, a private Kaggle script-kernel derived from `vladkuznetsov266/transformer-inference-example` to benchmark the model artifact inference speed directly. Version 2 completed on Tesla T4 with `torch=2.10.0+cu128`, `backend=fast`; best direct forward was `batch=2048`, `734786.8` candidates/s, and searcher-like `batch_process` for `65536` rows with `eval_batch_size=16384` was `630697.0` candidates/s. Evidence is recorded in `test_results/transformer_inference_example_kaggle_speed_2026-07-01.md`.

## 2026-06-30
- Added `tools/stream1_transformer_torch_benchmark.py`, a plain PyTorch fp16 Stream1 piece-transformer inference benchmark over the exported weight files. In local Docker `cmz-native-dev:2026-05-26` on RTX 3070 Laptop GPU, reference validation passed with max score-key error `26`; best eager SDPA point was `batch=2048`, `613885.6` candidates/s, with larger batches dropping sharply. Results are recorded in `test_results/stream1_transformer_torch_benchmark_2026-06-30.md` and `test_results/stream1_transformer_torch_benchmark_large_2026-06-30.md`.
- Optimized Stream1 `piece_transformer` inference hot path after Nsight profiling: removed per-thread `State128` copies in token build, added a `cols==256` LayerNorm fast path, added an<truncated omitted_approx_tokens="1371" />UDA allocations on exceptions. Verification recorded in `test_results/stream1_transformer_loader_2026-06-29.md`.
- Added the Stream1 piece-transformer host loader path and scratch arena scaffolding without wiring transformer inference. The weight loader now parses and validates the exact p900 piece-transformer manifest contract, loads exported transformer tensors and piece layout tables with exact byte sizes, exposes host/device/scratch byte helpers, and keeps MLP loading on an explicit separate branch. Verification recorded in `test_results/stream1_transformer_loader_2026-06-29.md`.
- Added Stream1 piece-transformer export tooling: an auto-detecting tools/export_stream1.py wrapper and tools/export_stream1_transformer.py for Kaggle p900 PilgrimPieceTransformer checkpoints. The exporter writes fast-slot input tables, piece layout tensors, Transformer block tensors, manifests with backend=piece_transformer, rejects non-24-output, non-4-layer, and non-1024-FF variants, and supports optional CPU fp32 reference JSON generation. Verification recorded in test_results/stream1_transformer_exporter_2026-06-29.md.
- Added tagged Stream1 model backend config constants and transformer metadata fields, preserving existing MLP defaults. Stream1 row-mode helpers now force the piece-transformer backend to parent rows while keeping MLP one-output child-row behavior, with contract coverage recorded in `test_results/stream1_piece_transformer_task1_2026-06-29.md`. Unknown Stream1 backend values now fail closed in row-mode helpers, MLP weight validation, and manifest backend parsing; legacy manifests without `backend` still default to MLP.

# Work With Kaggle

Use this skill whenever the task involves Kaggle notebooks, kernels, datasets, or GPU validation runs.

## Project Memory First

For project repositories, read local project guidance before changing notebooks or source:

- `AGENTS.md`
- `memory/PROMPTS.md` and `memory/CHANGELOG.md`, especially recent Kaggle entries
- relevant `test_results/kaggle_*` reports for the same failure/config family

This project has many Kaggle-specific decisions preserved in memory. Do not assume a generic Kaggle workflow is correct when project memory says otherwise.

## Safety And Scope

- Do not upload or publish current uncommitted source to a Kaggle dataset unless the user explicitly approves external export.
- Prefer GitHub-backed Kaggle source when the user has selected GitHub as source of truth.
- Do not push a public Kaggle notebook/kernel unless the user explicitly approves publication or public push.
- Do not make C++/CUDA algorithmic changes while diagnosing Kaggle failures unless the user explicitly approves code changes. Config-only notebook changes are acceptable when useful and consistent with the request.
- Do not revert unrelated local changes. Kaggle notebook edits often coexist with dirty source changes.
- For multi-rank validation, do not fake `WORLD_SIZE=2` on one GPU with both ranks on `LO<truncated omitted_approx_tokens="684" />stop the run and inspect downloaded logs. This rule came from project memory and applies to diagnostic/watch tasks.
- Do not stop production/no-timeout runs unless the user explicitly asks or the notebook itself has a configured timeout.
- If a run appears hung because stdout is redirected, check rank log files and whether live-rank streaming is enabled before assuming a stall.
- Preserve logs even when stopping: terminate gracefully when possible, then download output files.

## Failure Diagnosis Checklist

After a Kaggle failure, collect and scan:

- Kaggle worker status and kernel version
- notebook stdout tail
- rank logs under the notebook output directory
- result JSONL/CSV summaries
- GPU budget/preflight output
- explicit Kaggle messages such as disk quota failures

Common patterns in this project:

- `KernelWorkerStatus.ERROR` plus "more disk space than is available" usually means disk quota/static history arena pressure.
- `return_code=-9` can indicate host RAM OOM.
- `code=3002` / `STREAM_FATAL_STREAM3_DOUBLE_BUFFER_OVERFLOW` points to Stream3/Stream4/threshold/capacity flow diagnostics.
- `final selected count does not match score phase counts` points to final selection/histogram/exact-count mismatch.
- `cudaGraphInstantiate: out of memory` may require config-only headroom/shard-capacity changes before deeper code work.
- Silent output after build may simply mean rank stdout is redirected and live rank logging is disabled.

Write a short report under `test_results/` for meaningful Kaggle validations, sweeps, failures, or launches.

## Response Style

- Be explicit about whether you changed source code, notebook config only, or only launched/monitored a run.
- Include Kaggle kernel slug/version/status when known.
- Include exact local report/log paths in `test_results/`.
- Keep recommendations tied to evidence from logs, not guesses.
- If the next step requires exporting source or publishing publicly, ask for explicit approval first.

# Stream1 Piece Transformer PyTorch Gap Analysis - 2026-07-02

## Question

Explain why the native Stream1 piece-transformer backend is slower than the
PyTorch fast path on Kaggle T4, even though the native MLP backend is faster
than its PyTorch equivalent.

## Evidence

### PyTorch model path

The Kaggle artifact `vladkuznetsov266/megaminx-qtransformer-1782210824`
uses the model code under:

- `test_results/kaggle_model_artifact_download/megaminx-transformer/pilgrim/model.py`

The fast transformer block does:

1. `LayerNorm`
2. one `F.linear(..., in_proj_weight, in_proj_bias)` for QKV
3. reshape Q, K, V to `[batch, heads, seq, head_dim]`
4. one `F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, dropout_p=0.0, is_causal=False)`
5. one output `F.linear`
6. residual add
7. `LayerNorm`
8. `Linear -> SiLU -> Linear`
9. residual add

The piece input fast path precomputes:

- `fast_slot_projected`
- `fast_piece_static`
- `fast_piece_masks`

So the PyTorch speed is not from a different model. It is the same folded
piece-token construction idea plus PyTorch's optimized SDPA and linear kernels.

PyTorch documents `scaled_dot_product_attention` as an efficient implementation
which can automatically select optimized CUDA kernels, including FlashAttention
and memory-efficient attention, when the input supports them:

- https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.12/generated/torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention.html
- https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.12/backends.html

### Native Stream1 path

The current native code in `cuda/stream1.cu` still decomposes attention:

1. `stream1_transformer_add_qkv_bias_kernel`
2. `stream1_transformer_qk_batched_launch`
   - loops over 8 heads
   - launches CUTLASS `GemmBatched` per head
3. `stream1_transformer_pack_v51_kernel`
4. `stream1_transformer_softmax51_kernel`
5. `stream<truncated omitted_approx_tokens="568" />

## Root Cause

The native transformer backend is slower because its attention is not equivalent
to PyTorch's fused SDPA execution strategy.

PyTorch pays for one high-level SDPA call per layer and lets CUDA backend
dispatch pick a fused attention implementation when possible. Our native path
materializes and reloads intermediate attention tensors across many kernels:

- QKV bias is separate from QKV GEMM.
- QK is launched once per head.
- softmax is a separate global-memory pass.
- V is repacked into scratch.
- PV is launched once per head.
- residual/bias and SiLU epilogues are separate kernels.

The current native implementation uses tensor cores for QK/PV GEMMs, but it
still loses on launch count, global-memory roundtrips, and per-head
fragmentation. On T4 this overhead dominates enough that PyTorch is faster.

## What To Do Next

Do not add a PyTorch fallback. The native transformer backend needs a better
attention backend.

Priority order:

1. Capture a bounded PyTorch profiler or Nsight trace on Kaggle T4 for exactly
   one warmed direct-forward batch, to record actual SDPA kernel names.
2. Add a bounded capture mode to `stream_benchmark` so Nsight profiles one
   `B_MICRO=512, concurrency=2` group instead of the broad sweep.
3. Replace per-head QK + softmax + V-pack + per-head PV with a native fused
   short-SDPA backend for fixed `seq_len=51`, `head_dim=32`, `nhead=8`.
4. Fuse epilogues where possible:
   - QKV GEMM + bias
   - FF1 GEMM + bias + SiLU
   - attention output GEMM + residual + bias
   - FF2 GEMM + residual + bias
5. Keep the MLP path separate and unchanged.

## Current Confidence

High. The code-path comparison and Kaggle measurements agree. The missing
piece is exact PyTorch CUDA kernel names on Kaggle T4, but the root cause does
not depend on those names: PyTorch uses a single SDPA abstraction, while native
currently decomposes attention into many launch and scratch stages.

# Stream1 Piece Transformer PyTorch Gap Analysis - 2026-07-02

## Question

Explain why the native Stream1 piece-transformer backend is slower than the
PyTorch fast path on Kaggle T4, even though the native MLP backend is faster
than its PyTorch equivalent.

## Evidence

### PyTorch model path

The Kaggle artifact `vladkuznetsov266/megaminx-qtransformer-1782210824`
uses the model code under:

- `test_results/kaggle_model_artifact_download/megaminx-transformer/pilgrim/model.py`

The fast transformer block does:

1. `LayerNorm`
2. one `F.linear(..., in_proj_weight, in_proj_bias)` for QKV
3. reshape Q, K, V to `[batch, heads, seq, head_dim]`
4. one `F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, dropout_p=0.0, is_causal=False)`
5. one output `F.linear`
6. residual add
7. `LayerNorm`
8. `Linear -> SiLU -> Linear`
9. residual add

The piece input fast path precomputes:

- `fast_slot_projected`
- `fast_piece_static`
- `fast_piece_masks`

So the PyTorch speed is not from a different model. It is the same folded
piece-token construction idea plus PyTorch's optimized SDPA and linear kernels.

PyTorch documents `scaled_dot_product_attention` as an efficient implementation
which can automatically select optimized CUDA kernels, including FlashAttention
and memory-efficient attention, when the input supports them:

- https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.12/generated/torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention.html
- https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.12/backends.html

### Native Stream1 path

The current native code in `cuda/stream1.cu` still decomposes attention:

1. `stream1_transformer_add_qkv_bias_kernel`
2. `stream1_transformer_qk_batched_launch`
   - loops over 8 heads
   - launches CUTLASS `GemmBatched` per head
3. `stream1_transformer_pack_v51_kernel`
4. `stream1_transformer_softmax51_kernel`
5. `stream<truncated omitted_approx_tokens="568" />

## Root Cause

The native transformer backend is slower because its attention is not equivalent
to PyTorch's fused SDPA execution strategy.

PyTorch pays for one high-level SDPA call per layer and lets CUDA backend
dispatch pick a fused attention implementation when possible. Our native path
materializes and reloads intermediate attention tensors across many kernels:

- QKV bias is separate from QKV GEMM.
- QK is launched once per head.
- softmax is a separate global-memory pass.
- V is repacked into scratch.
- PV is launched once per head.
- residual/bias and SiLU epilogues are separate kernels.

The current native implementation uses tensor cores for QK/PV GEMMs, but it
still loses on launch count, global-memory roundtrips, and per-head
fragmentation. On T4 this overhead dominates enough that PyTorch is faster.

## What To Do Next

Do not add a PyTorch fallback. The native transformer backend needs a better
attention backend.

Priority order:

1. Capture a bounded PyTorch profiler or Nsight trace on Kaggle T4 for exactly
   one warmed direct-forward batch, to record actual SDPA kernel names.
2. Add a bounded capture mode to `stream_benchmark` so Nsight profiles one
   `B_MICRO=512, concurrency=2` group instead of the broad sweep.
3. Replace per-head QK + softmax + V-pack + per-head PV with a native fused
   short-SDPA backend for fixed `seq_len=51`, `head_dim=32`, `nhead=8`.
4. Fuse epilogues where possible:
   - QKV GEMM + bias
   - FF1 GEMM + bias + SiLU
   - attention output GEMM + residual + bias
   - FF2 GEMM + residual + bias
5. Keep the MLP path separate and unchanged.

## Current Confidence

High. The code-path comparison and Kaggle measurements agree. The missing
piece is exact PyTorch CUDA kernel names on Kaggle T4, but the root cause does
not depend on those names: PyTorch uses a single SDPA abstraction, while native
currently decomposes attention into many launch and scratch stages.

- Fixed the Torch-side Stream1 MLP benchmark parser to accept `initial_state_id` from `data/test.csv`, matching the native benchmark input schema. Kaggle 2xT4 v1 had completed native CUTLASS MLP measurements but failed before Torch timing because the parser only accepted `id/puzzle_id/ID`. Evidence: `test_results/kaggle_t4_mlp_native_vs_torch_v1_failure_2026-07-01.md`.
- Ran Kaggle 2xT4 MLP native-vs-PyTorch benchmark version 2 against source tag `stream1-mlp-torch-kaggle-v2-code` (`cc90a3d`). Kaggle completed successfully. Best native CUTLASS MLP reached `16.42M` candidates/s on GPU0 and `15.73M` on GPU1; best PyTorch preindexed MLP reached `8.13M` and `6.76M` candidates/s. Native is `2.02x`/`2.33x` faster per GPU and `2.16x` faster in aggregate. Evidence: `test_results/stream1_mlp_native_vs_torch_kaggle_v2_2026-07-01.md`.
- Added kaggle_transformer_inference_speed/transformer_inference_profile.py and test_results/stream1_transformer_pytorch_gap_analysis_2026-07-02.md to compare the PyTorch fast SDPA path against the native Stream1 piece-transformer path. The analysis identifies native attention decomposition, per-head QK/PV launches, separate softmax/V-pack, and unfused epilogues as the current T4 performance gap; no solver runtime or MLP path behavior changed.
- Added an explicit Stream1 piece-transformer attention backend split: fp16 uses the existing T4/SM75-safe CUTLASS tensor QK/softmax/PV path, while bf16 on SM80+ routes to a separate `cuda/stream1_transformer_fmha.cu` CUTLASS example-41 FMHA path with packed BMHK Q/K/V. The piece-transformer executor now lives in `cuda/stream1_transformer.cu`, leaving the MLP Stream1 implementation in `cuda/stream1.cu`; this gives the fused-transformer work a separate backend boundary for future epilogue/layout/graph optimization. The FMHA code is fail-closed when CUTLASS FMHA headers or SM80+ are unavailable, and the MLP path is not touched. Verification passed `stream1_transformer_cuda_tests`, `contract_tests`, and `dispatcher_cuda_tests`; bf16 FMHA smoke also passed after the split. Evidence: `test_results/stream1_transformer_cutlass_fmha_backend_split_2026-07-02.md`. Local performance numbers were gathered on a throttled RTX 3070 Laptop GPU and should not be treated as an A100/T4 performance gate.

- Added a transformer-local residual GEMM epilogue path in `cuda/stream1_transformer.cu` for attention-output and FF2 projections: CUTLASS now computes `D = A * B + residual`, followed by a narrow bias-add kernel. This removes the previous large intermediate branch materialization for those residual projections, leaves the MLP path untouched, and keeps fp16/T4 and bf16/FMHA backend selection fail-closed. Verification passed `stream1_transformer_cuda_tests`, `contract_tests`, and `dispatcher_cuda_tests`; local smoke reports reached `575995.4` candidates/s for fp16 staged `512x1` and `675808.8` candidates/s for bf16 FMHA `512x1`. Evidence: `test_results/stream1_transformer_cutlass_fmha_backend_split_2026-07-02.md`.

- Fused the Stream1 piece-transformer FF1 projection epilogue in `cuda/stream1_transformer.cu`: CUTLASS now computes `GEMM + bias + SiLU` through `GemmUniversalWithBroadcast` and `LinearCombinationBiasElementwise`, while the MLP path and residual GEMM path remain separate. Local Docker verification passed `stream1_transformer_cuda_tests`, `contract_tests`, and `dispatcher_cuda_tests`; Kaggle 2xT4 v8 against commit `3bf864a` improved best T4 throughput from `408179.9/405676.1` to `446292.4/448865.3` candidates/s. Evidence: `test_results/stream1_transformer_ff1_fused_2026-07-03.md` and `test_results/stream1_transformer_kaggle_benchmark_v8_ff1_fused_2026-07-03.md`.

    const half* qkv_bias,
    half* packed_qkv,
    half* context,
    Stream1TransformerDims dims,
    std::uint32_t b_micro,
    cudaStream_t stream) {
    if (dims.seq_len != FMHA_SEQ51 || dims.d_model != FMHA_DMODEL256 ||
        dims.nhead != FMHA_NHEAD8 || dims.head_dim != FMHA_HEAD_DIM32) {
        throw std::invalid_argument("Stream1 piece_transformer CUTLASS FMHA requires seq_len=51 d_model=256 nhead=8 head_dim=32");
    }
    if (qkv == nullptr || qkv_bias == nullptr || packed_qkv == nullptr || context == nullptr) {
        throw std::invalid_argument("Stream1 piece_transformer CUTLASS FMHA requires qkv, qkv_bias, packed_qkv, and context");
    }
#if BEAM_HAS_CUTLASS && BEAM_HAS_CUTLASS_FMHA
    const std::uint64_t qkv_total = static_cast<std::uint64_t>(b_micro) * FMHA_SEQ51 * FMHA_QKV_STRIDE51;
    stream1_transformer_fmha_pack_qkv_bmhk51_kernel<<<
        static_cast<unsigned>((qkv_total + 255ULL) / 256ULL),
        256,
        0,
        stream>>>(qkv, qkv_bias, packed_qkv, dims.dtype, b_micro);
    if (dims.dtype == STREAM1_DTYPE_BF16) {
        stream1_transformer_fmha_launch_typed<cutlass::bfloat16_t, cutlass::arch::Sm80>(packed_qkv, context, b_micro, stream);
        return;
    }
    if (dims.dtype == STREAM1_DTYPE_FP16) {
        stream1_transformer_fmha_launch_typed<cutlass::half_t, cutlass::arch::Sm80>(packed_qkv, context, b_micro, stream);
        return;
    }
    throw std::invalid_argument("Stream1 piece_transformer CUTLASS FMHA dtype must be fp16 or bf16");
#else
    (void)qkv;
    (void)qkv_bias;
    (void)packed_qkv;
    (void)context;
    (void)dims;
    (void)b_micro;
    (void)stream;
    throw std::invalid_argument("Stream1 piece_transformer CUTLASS FMHA requires CUTLASS example 41 headers");
#endif
}

} // namespace beam

__global__ void stream1_transformer_add_qkv_bias_kernel(
    half* __restrict__ qkv,
    const half* __restrict__ qkv_bias,
    std::uint32_t dtype,
    std::uint32_t b_micro) {
    const std::uint64_t i = static_cast<std::uint64_t>(blockIdx.x) * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;
    const std::uint64_t total = static_cast<std::uint64_t>(b_micro) *

        stream1_transformer_load_scalar_device(qkv_bias, col, dtype);

## Source

- Kaggle kernel: `trydotatwo/cayley-beam-transformer-2xt4-benchmark`, version 9.

- Backend: native Stream1 piece-transformer fp16 path.
- Change under test: QKV projection fused as CUTLASS GEMM + bias, on top of the previous FF1 GEMM + bias + SiLU fusion.

Downloaded outputs:

- `test_results/kaggle_stream1_transformer_2xt4_v9_qkv_fused_2026-07-03/stream1_transformer_benchmark_rows.csv`

  - PyTorch direct forward best: `734786.8` candidates/s.

- The QKV bias epilogue is a real improvement, but the remaining gap is still in the transformer attention/layout/remaining epilogues rather than FF1/QKV bias alone.

## Source

- Kaggle kernel: `trydotatwo/cayley-beam-transformer-2xt4-benchmark`, version 9.

- Change under test: QKV projection fused as CUTLASS GEMM + bias, on top of the previous FF1 GEMM + bias + SiLU fusion.

Downloaded outputs:

- `test_results/kaggle_stream1_transformer_2xt4_v9_qkv_fused_2026-07-03/stream1_transformer_benchmark_rows.csv`

  - PyTorch direct forward best: `734786.8` candidates/s.

- The QKV bias epilogue is a real improvement, but the remaining gap is still in the transformer attention/layout/remaining epilogues rather than FF1/QKV bias alone.

# HighloadGpu

Router for CUDA code-writing and high-performance GPU engineering. Default to a single-GPU CUDA hot path first; use multi-GPU or search/decoding guidance only when the task calls for it.

## Pick The Sub-Skill

- CUDA kernels, memory layout, CUTLASS/CUB, graphs, native hot paths: `write-cuda-hot-paths`
- Beam search, top-k/top-p decoding, frontier expansion, candidate selection: `optimize-gpu-search-and-decoding`
- Multi-GPU scaling, rank ownership, peer access, NCCL, overlap: `design-multigpu-systems`
- Python/Rust/C++/CUDA ownership boundaries: `choose-stack-boundaries`
- GPU model, compute capability, CUDA/library docs: `use-nvidia-docs`
- Timeline/stream/NCCL/launch gaps: `use-nsight-systems`
- One-kernel bottleneck: `use-nsight-compute`
- Illegal access/race/init/sync bug: `use-compute-sanitizer`
- Batch/concurrency/shard sweeps: `benchmark-and-sweep-gpu-configs`
- Kaggle/Molab/remote GPU profiling: `profile-remote-gpu-runs`

## Defaults

- Python: wrappers, notebooks, dashboards, CLI/torchrun launch.
- Rust: safe config, validation, artifact/log tooling, host services.
- C++ + CUDA: CPU/GPU hot paths, kernels, CUDA Graphs, NCCL, CUTLASS, CUB/CCCL.

Check current NVIDIA docs before hardware-specific advice. Require correctness checks and profiling evidence before architecture changes.

name: write-cuda-hot-paths
description: Use when writing or optimizing CUDA kernels, memory layouts, and GPU hot paths.

# Write CUDA Hot Paths

Primary skill for CUDA code-writing. Hot paths are fixed-capacity, allocation-free, profiler-driven, and explicit about layout, alignment, ownership, and synchronization.

## Workflow

1. State shapes, precision, target GPU, correctness oracle, and measured bottleneck.
2. Choose library vs custom kernel; use custom CUDA where layout, fusion, or control flow makes it worthwhile.
3. Design layout first, implement a small deterministic path, then profile.

## Rules

- Allocate device memory, library temp, NCCL buffers, and graph resources before repeated loops.
- Use explicit capacity guards; fail loudly on overflow.
- Keep CPU readback out of the steady-state path.
- Use CUDA Graphs for repeated launch templates; keep dynamic dispatch on host.
- Add static asserts for cross-kernel metadata size/alignment.
- Store only downstream-needed data; avoid materializing large intermediates when compact keys, indices, or reductions are enough.

## Library Defaults

CUTLASS/cuBLAS for GEMM/tensor-core kernels; CUB/CCCL for sort/reduce/scan/select; NCCL for GPU exchange/collectives; CUDA Runtime/Driver APIs for memory, streams, events, graphs, devices, and peer access.

## Avoid

Dynamic `cudaMalloc`, Python data-plane loops, fine-grained atomics when partition/sort/scan works, custom sort before checking CUB/CCCL, and synchronization that hides ownership bugs.

# Systematic Debugging

## Overview

Random fixes waste time and create new bugs. Quick patches mask underlying issues.

**Core principle:** ALWAYS find root cause before attempting fixes. Symptom fixes are failure.

**Violating the letter of this process is violating the spirit of debugging.**

## The Iron Law

```
NO FIXES WITHOUT ROOT CAUSE INVESTIGATION FIRST
```

If you haven't completed Phase 1, you cannot propose fixes.

## When to Use

Use for ANY technical issue:
- Test failures
- Bugs in production
- Unexpected behavior
- Performance problems
- Build failures
- Integration issues

**Use this ESPECIALLY when:**
- Under time pressure (emergencies make guessing tempting)
- "Just one quick fix" seems obvious
- You've already tried multiple fixes
- Previous fix didn't work
- You don't fully understand the issue

**Don't skip when:**
- Issue seems simple (simple bugs have root causes too)
- You're in a hurry (rushing guarantees rework)
- Manager wants it fixed NOW (systematic is faster than thrashing)

## The Four Phases

You MUST complete each phase before proceeding to the next.

### Phase 1: Root Cause Investigation

**BEFORE attempting ANY fix:**

1. **Read Error Messages Carefully**
   - Don't skip past errors or warnings
   - They often contain the exact solution
   - Read stack traces completely
   - Note line numbers, file paths, error codes

2. **Reproduce Consistently**
   - Can you trigger it reliably?
   - What are the exact steps?
   - Does it happen every time?
   - If not reproducible в†’ gather more data, don't guess

3. **Check Recent Changes**
   - What changed that could cause this?
   - Git diff, recent commits
   - New dependencies, config changes
   - Environmental differen<truncated omitted_approx_tokens="1512" />|
| "Reference too long, I'll adapt the pattern" | Partial understanding guarantees bugs. Read it completely. |
| "I see the problem, let me fix it" | Seeing symptoms в‰  understanding root cause. |
| "One more fix attempt" (after 2+ failures) | 3+ failures = architectural problem. Question pattern, don't fix again. |

## Quick Reference

| Phase | Key Activities | Success Criteria |
|-------|---------------|------------------|
| **1. Root Cause** | Read errors, reproduce, check changes, gather evidence | Understand WHAT and WHY |
| **2. Pattern** | Find working examples, compare | Identify differences |
| **3. Hypothesis** | Form theory, test minimally | Confirmed or new hypothesis |
| **4. Implementation** | Create test, fix, verify | Bug resolved, tests pass |

## When Process Reveals "No Root Cause"

If systematic investigation reveals issue is truly environmental, timing-dependent, or external:

1. You've completed the process
2. Document what you investigated
3. Implement appropriate handling (retry, timeout, error message)
4. Add monitoring/logging for future investigation

**But:** 95% of "no root cause" cases are incomplete investigation.

## Supporting Techniques

These techniques are part of systematic debugging and available in this directory:

- **`root-cause-tracing.md`** - Trace bugs backward through call stack to find original trigger
- **`defense-in-depth.md`** - Add validation at multiple layers after finding root cause
- **`condition-based-waiting.md`** - Replace arbitrary timeouts with condition polling

**Related skills:**
- **superpowers:test-driven-development** - For creating failing test case (Phase 4, Step 1)
- **superpowers:verification-before-completion** - Verify fix worked before claiming success

## Real-World Impact

From debugging sessions:
- Systematic approach: 15-30 minutes to fix
- Random fixes approach: 2-3 hours of thrashing
- First-time fix rate: 95% vs 40%
- New bugs introduced: Near zero vs common

## Overview

Random fixes waste time and create new bugs. Quick patches mask underlying issues.

**Core principle:** ALWAYS find root cause before attempting fixes. Symptom fixes are failure.

**Violating the letter of this process is violating the spirit of debugging.**

## The Iron Law

```
NO FIXES WITHOUT ROOT CAUSE INVESTIGATION FIRST
```

If you haven't completed Phase 1, you cannot propose fixes.

## When to Use

Use for ANY technical issue:
- Test failures
- Bugs in production
- Unexpected behavior
- Performance problems
- Build failures
- Integration issues

**Use this ESPECIALLY when:**
- Under time pressure (emergencies make guessing tempting)
- "Just one quick fix" seems obvious
- You've already tried multiple fixes
- Previous fix didn't work
- You don't fully understand the issue

**Don't skip when:**
- Issue seems simple (simple bugs have root causes too)
- You're in a hurry (rushing guarantees rework)
- Manager wants it fixed NOW (systematic is faster than thrashing)

## The Four Phases

You MUST complete each phase before proceeding to the next.

### Phase 1: Root Cause Investigation

**BEFORE attempting ANY fix:**

1. **Read Error Messages Carefully**
   - Don't skip past errors or warnings
   - They often contain the exact solution
   - Read stack traces completely
   - Note line numbers, file paths, error codes

2. **Reproduce Consistently**
   - Can you trigger it reliably?
   - What are the exact steps?
   - Does it happen every time?
   - If not reproducible в†’ gather more data, don't guess

3. **Check Recent Changes**
   - What changed that could cause this?
   - Git diff, recent commits
   - New dependencies, config changes
   - Environmental differen<truncated omitted_approx_tokens="1512" />|
| "Reference too long, I'll adapt the pattern" | Partial understanding guarantees bugs. Read it completely. |
| "I see the problem, let me fix it" | Seeing symptoms в‰  understanding root cause. |
| "One more fix attempt" (after 2+ failures) | 3+ failures = architectural problem. Question pattern, don't fix again. |

## Quick Reference

| Phase | Key Activities | Success Criteria |
|-------|---------------|------------------|
| **1. Root Cause** | Read errors, reproduce, check changes, gather evidence | Understand WHAT and WHY |
| **2. Pattern** | Find working examples, compare | Identify differences |
| **3. Hypothesis** | Form theory, test minimally | Confirmed or new hypothesis |
| **4. Implementation** | Create test, fix, verify | Bug resolved, tests pass |

## When Process Reveals "No Root Cause"

If systematic investigation reveals issue is truly environmental, timing-dependent, or external:

1. You've completed the process
2. Document what you investigated
3. Implement appropriate handling (retry, timeout, error message)
4. Add monitoring/logging for future investigation

**But:** 95% of "no root cause" cases are incomplete investigation.

## Supporting Techniques

These techniques are part of systematic debugging and available in this directory:

- **`root-cause-tracing.md`** - Trace bugs backward through call stack to find original trigger
- **`defense-in-depth.md`** - Add validation at multiple layers after finding root cause
- **`condition-based-waiting.md`** - Replace arbitrary timeouts with condition polling

**Related skills:**
- **superpowers:test-driven-development** - For creating failing test case (Phase 4, Step 1)
- **superpowers:verification-before-completion** - Verify fix worked before claiming success

## Real-World Impact

From debugging sessions:
- Systematic approach: 15-30 minutes to fix
- Random fixes approach: 2-3 hours of thrashing
- First-time fix rate: 95% vs 40%
- New bugs introduced: Near zero vs common

__global__ void stream1_transformer_bias_silu_kernel(
    half* __restrict__ matrix,
    const half* __restrict__ bias,
    std::uint32_t rows,
    std::uint32_t cols,
    std::uint32_t dtype) {
    const std::uint32_t i = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;
    const std::uint32_t total = rows * cols;
    if (i >= total) {
        return;
    }
    const std::uint32_t col = i % cols;
    const float x = stream1_transformer_load_scalar_device(matrix, i, dtype) +
        stream1_transformer_load_scalar_device(bias, col, dtype);
    const float y = x / (1.0f + expf(-x));
    stream1_transformer_store_scalar_device(matrix, i, y, dtype);
}

__global__ void stream1_transformer_bias_add_kernel(
    half* __restrict__ matrix,
    const half* __restrict__ bias,
    std::uint32_t rows,
    std::uint32_t cols,
    std::uint32_t dtype) {
    const std::uint32_t i = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;
    const std::uint32_t total = rows * cols;
    if (i >= total) {
        return;
    }
    const std::uint32_t col = i % cols;
    const float x = stream1_transformer_load_scalar_device(matrix, i, dtype) +
        stream1_transformer_load_scalar_device(bias, col, dtype);
    stream1_transformer_store_scalar_device(matrix, i, x, dtype);
}

__global__ void stream1_transformer_bias_silu_kernel(
    half* __restrict__ matrix,
    const half* __restrict__ bias,
    std::uint32_t rows,
    std::uint32_t cols,
    std::uint32_t dtype) {
    const std::uint32_t i = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;
    const std::uint32_t total = rows * cols;
    if (i >= total) {
        return;
    }
    const std::uint32_t col = i % cols;
    const float x = stream1_transformer_load_scalar_device(matrix, i, dtype) +
        stream1_transformer_load_scalar_device(bias, col, dtype);
    const float y = x / (1.0f + expf(-x));
    stream1_transformer_store_scalar_device(matrix, i, y, dtype);
}

__global__ void stream1_transformer_bias_add_kernel(
    half* __restrict__ matrix,
    const half* __restrict__ bias,
    std::uint32_t rows,
    std::uint32_t cols,
    std::uint32_t dtype) {
    const std::uint32_t i = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;
    const std::uint32_t total = rows * cols;
    if (i >= total) {
        return;
    }
    const std::uint32_t col = i % cols;
    const float x = stream1_transformer_load_scalar_device(matrix, i, dtype) +
        stream1_transformer_load_scalar_device(bias, col, dtype);
    stream1_transformer_store_scalar_device(matrix, i, x, dtype);
}

# Use Nsight Systems

Use Nsight Systems for stream idle gaps, CPU launch/sync blocks, and NCCL/compute overlap.

```bash
nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt,cublas,nccl --stats=true --force-overwrite=true -o nsys_run ./runner ...

```

Profile a bounded window. Add NVTX around batch, stage, stream, rank, shard, communication, and pipeline phase.

# Profile Remote GPU Runs

## Routing

Use `work-with-kaggle` or `work-with-molab` for platform operations when available. Use HighloadGpu for architecture/profiling decisions.

## Rules

- Do not leak tokenized session URLs.
- Do not interrupt production/no-timeout runs unless asked.
- Probe `nvidia-smi`, RAM, disk, CUDA Toolkit, compiler, and packages.
- If Nsight is unavailable, use internal timers, NVTX where possible, and structured JSONL logs.
- Keep transient build/checkouts in temp; save final logs/CSVs/PNGs to output and project `test_results/`.
- Verify arch flags from docs/environment.

__device__ float stream1_transformer_warp_reduce_sum_device(float value) {
    constexpr unsigned mask = 0xffffffffU;
    for (int offset = 16; offset > 0; offset >>= 1) {
        value += __shfl_down_sync(mask, value, offset);
    }
    return __shfl_sync(mask, value, 0);
}

__device__ float stream1_transformer_warp_reduce_max_device(float value) {
    constexpr unsigned mask = 0xffffffffU;
    for (int offset = 16; offset > 0; offset >>= 1) {
        value = fmaxf(value, __shfl_down_sync(mask, value, offset));
    }
    return __shfl_sync(mask, value, 0);
}

__device__ std::uint32_t stream1_transformer_score_key_from_float_device(float q) {
    q = fminf(fmaxf(q, 0.0f), SCORE_MAX_Q);
    return static_cast<std::uint32_t>(rintf(q * static_cast<float>(SCORE_SCALE)));
}

__device__ float stream1_transformer_load_scalar_device(const half* ptr, std::uint64_t idx, std::uint32_t dtype) {
    if (dtype == STREAM1_DTYPE_BF16) {
        return __bfloat162float(reinterpret_cast<const __nv_bfloat16*>(ptr)[idx]);
    }
    return __half2float(ptr[idx]);
}

__device__ float stream1_transformer_warp_reduce_sum_device(float value) {
    constexpr unsigned mask = 0xffffffffU;
    for (int offset = 16; offset > 0; offset >>= 1) {
        value += __shfl_down_sync(mask, value, offset);
    }
    return __shfl_sync(mask, value, 0);

__device__ float stream1_transformer_warp_reduce_max_device(float value) {
    constexpr unsigned mask = 0xffffffffU;
    for (int offset = 16; offset > 0; offset >>= 1) {
        value = fmaxf(value, __shfl_down_sync(mask, value, offset));
    }
    return __shfl_sync(mask, value, 0);
}

__device__ std::uint32_t stream1_transformer_score_key_from_float_device(float q) {
    q = fminf(fmaxf(q, 0.0f), SCORE_MAX_Q);

}

__global__ void stream1_transformer_pack_v51_kernel(
    const half* __restrict__ qkv,
    half* __restrict__ scores_probs,
    std::uint32_t dtype,

    const std::uint64_t i = static_cast<std::uint64_t>(blockIdx.x) * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;
    const std::uint64_t per_matrix = static_cast<std::uint64_t>(STREAM1_TRANSFORMER_HEAD_OUTPUT_STRIDE51);
    const std::uint64_t total = static_cast<std::uint64_t>(STREAM1_TRANSFORMER_NHEAD8) * b_micro * per_matrix;
    if (i >= total) {
        return;
    }
    const std::uint32_t lane = static_cast<std::uint32_t>(i % STREAM1_TRANSFORMER_HEAD_DIM32);
    const std::uint32_t key = static_cast<std::uint32_t>((i / STREAM1_TRANSFORMER_HEAD_DIM32) % STREAM1_TRANSFORMER_SCORE_ROW_STRIDE51);
    const std::uint64_t row_head = i / per_matrix;
    const std::uint32_t row = static_cast<std::uint32_t>(row_head % b_micro);
    const std::uint32_t head = static_cast<std::uint32_t>(row_head / b_micro);
    const std::uint64_t matrix_base =
        (static_cast<std::uint64_t>(head) * b_micro + row) * STREAM1_TRANSFORMER_SCORE_STRIDE51;
    float value = 0.0f;
    if (key < STREAM1_TRANSFORMER_SEQ51) {
        const std::uint64_t qkv_idx =
            static_cast<std::uint64_t>(row) * STREAM1_TRANSFORMER_SEQ51 * STREAM1_TRANSFORMER_QKV_STRIDE51 +

            2ULL * STREAM1_TRANSFORMER_DMODEL256 +

            lane;
        value = stream1_transformer_load_scalar_device(qkv, qkv_idx, dtype);
    }
    stream1_transformer_store_scalar_device(
        scores_probs,
        matrix_base + STREAM1_TRANSFORMER_PROB_STRIDE51 +
            static_cast<std::uint64_t>(key) * STREAM1_TRANSFORMER_HEAD_DIM32 + lane,
        value,
        dtype);
}

# Project Agent Rules

## Operating Rule
- Read `AGENTS.md` before project edits.
- Update `memory/CHANGELOG.md` after meaningful code, config, or architecture changes.
- Update `memory/PROMPTS.md` with user prompts that define requirements.
- Store test outputs, logs, and verification notes under `test_results/`.
- Prefer agent-centered code: explicit contracts, deterministic tests, small files, low hidden state.

## Architecture Source
- Primary architecture contract: `ARCHITECTURE_NEED.md`.
- Current Stream 4 implementation rule: use threshold + compact + CUB/fixed-temp sort/reduce + compact; do not use Stream 4 hash-table dedup.

## Implementation Guardrails
- `State128` logical bytes are `v[0..119]`.
- `State128` padding bytes are `v[120..127]`.
- Persistent frontier padding must be zero.
- `FinalResponse` may temporarily store `target_local_idx` in `v[120..123]`.
- `Hash128` is one logical 128-bit key stored as `{lo, hi}`.
- `CandidateMeta` must remain 32 bytes and 32-byte aligned.
- Stream 3 payload id must be original candidate id, not compact index.
- Stream 4 must not apply shard top-k or semantic shard cap.

# HighloadGpu

Router for CUDA code-writing and high-performance GPU engineering. Default to a single-GPU CUDA hot path first; use multi-GPU or search/decoding guidance only when the task calls for it.

## Pick The Sub-Skill

- CUDA kernels, memory layout, CUTLASS/CUB, graphs, native hot paths: `write-cuda-hot-paths`
- Beam search, top-k/top-p decoding, frontier expansion, candidate selection: `optimize-gpu-search-and-decoding`
- Multi-GPU scaling, rank ownership, peer access, NCCL, overlap: `design-multigpu-systems`
- Python/Rust/C++/CUDA ownership boundaries: `choose-stack-boundaries`
- GPU model, compute capability, CUDA/library docs: `use-nvidia-docs`
- Timeline/stream/NCCL/launch gaps: `use-nsight-systems`
- One-kernel bottleneck: `use-nsight-compute`
- Illegal access/race/init/sync bug: `use-compute-sanitizer`
- Batch/concurrency/shard sweeps: `benchmark-and-sweep-gpu-configs`
- Kaggle/Molab/remote GPU profiling: `profile-remote-gpu-runs`

## Defaults

- Python: wrappers, notebooks, dashboards, CLI/torchrun launch.
- Rust: safe config, validation, artifact/log tooling, host services.
- C++ + CUDA: CPU/GPU hot paths, kernels, CUDA Graphs, NCCL, CUTLASS, CUB/CCCL.

Check current NVIDIA docs before hardware-specific advice. Require correctness checks and profiling evidence before architecture changes.

name: write-cuda-hot-paths
description: Use when writing or optimizing CUDA kernels, memory layouts, and GPU hot paths.
---

# Write CUDA Hot Paths

Primary skill for CUDA code-writing. Hot paths are fixed-capacity, allocation-free, profiler-driven, and explicit about layout, alignment, ownership, and synchronization.

## Workflow

1. State shapes, precision, target GPU, correctness oracle, and measured bottleneck.
2. Choose library vs custom kernel; use custom CUDA where layout, fusion, or control flow makes it worthwhile.
3. Design layout first, implement a small deterministic path, then profile.

## Rules

- Allocate device memory, library temp, NCCL buffers, and graph resources before repeated loops.
- Use explicit capacity guards; fail loudly on overflow.
- Keep CPU readback out of the steady-state path.
- Use CUDA Graphs for repeated launch templates; keep dynamic dispatch on host.
- Add static asserts for cross-kernel metadata size/alignment.
- Store only downstream-needed data; avoid materializing large intermediates when compact keys, indices, or reductions are enough.

## Library Defaults

CUTLASS/cuBLAS for GEMM/tensor-core kernels; CUB/CCCL for sort/reduce/scan/select; NCCL for GPU exchange/collectives; CUDA Runtime/Driver APIs for memory, streams, events, graphs, devices, and peer access.

## Avoid

Dynamic `cudaMalloc`, Python data-plane loops, fine-grained atomics when partition/sort/scan works, custom sort before checking CUB/CCCL, and synchronization that hides ownership bugs.

# Systematic Debugging

## Overview

Random fixes waste time and create new bugs. Quick patches mask underlying issues.

**Core principle:** ALWAYS find root cause before attempting fixes. Symptom fixes are failure.

**Violating the letter of this process is violating the spirit of debugging.**

## The Iron Law

```
NO FIXES WITHOUT ROOT CAUSE INVESTIGATION FIRST
```

If you haven't completed Phase 1, you cannot propose fixes.

## When to Use

Use for ANY technical issue:
- Test failures
- Bugs in production
- Unexpected behavior
- Performance problems
- Build failures
- Integration issues

**Use this ESPECIALLY when:**
- Under time pressure (emergencies make guessing tempting)
- "Just one quick fix" seems obvious
- You've already tried multiple fixes
- Previous fix didn't work
- You don't fully understand the issue

**Don't skip when:**
- Issue seems simple (simple bugs have root causes too)
- You're in a hurry (rushing guarantees rework)
- Manager wants it fixed NOW (systematic is faster than thrashing)

## The Four Phases

You MUST complete each phase before proceeding to the next.

### Phase 1: Root Cause Investigation

**BEFORE attempting ANY fix:**

1. **Read Error Messages Carefully**
   - Don't skip past errors or warnings
   - They often contain the exact solution
   - Read stack traces completely
   - Note line numbers, file paths, error codes

2. **Reproduce Consistently**
   - Can you trigger it reliably?
   - What are the exact steps?
   - Does it happen every time?
   - If not reproducible в†’ gather more data, don't guess

3. **Check Recent Changes**
   - What changed that could cause this?
   - Git diff, recent commits
   - New dependencies, config changes
   - Environmental differen<truncated omitted_approx_tokens="1512" />|
| "Reference too long, I'll adapt the pattern" | Partial understanding guarantees bugs. Read it completely. |
| "I see the problem, let me fix it" | Seeing symptoms в‰  understanding root cause. |
| "One more fix attempt" (after 2+ failures) | 3+ failures = architectural problem. Question pattern, don't fix again. |

## Quick Reference

| Phase | Key Activities | Success Criteria |
|-------|---------------|------------------|
| **1. Root Cause** | Read errors, reproduce, check changes, gather evidence | Understand WHAT and WHY |
| **2. Pattern** | Find working examples, compare | Identify differences |
| **3. Hypothesis** | Form theory, test minimally | Confirmed or new hypothesis |
| **4. Implementation** | Create test, fix, verify | Bug resolved, tests pass |

## When Process Reveals "No Root Cause"

If systematic investigation reveals issue is truly environmental, timing-dependent, or external:

1. You've completed the process
2. Document what you investigated
3. Implement appropriate handling (retry, timeout, error message)
4. Add monitoring/logging for future investigation

**But:** 95% of "no root cause" cases are incomplete investigation.

## Supporting Techniques

These techniques are part of systematic debugging and available in this directory:

- **`root-cause-tracing.md`** - Trace bugs backward through call stack to find original trigger
- **`defense-in-depth.md`** - Add validation at multiple layers after finding root cause
- **`condition-based-waiting.md`** - Replace arbitrary timeouts with condition polling

**Related skills:**
- **superpowers:test-driven-development** - For creating failing test case (Phase 4, Step 1)
- **superpowers:verification-before-completion** - Verify fix worked before claiming success

## Real-World Impact

From debugging sessions:
- Systematic approach: 15-30 minutes to fix
- Random fixes approach: 2-3 hours of thrashing
- First-time fix rate: 95% vs 40%
- New bugs introduced: Near zero vs common

# Use Nsight Systems

Use Nsight Systems for stream idle gaps, CPU launch/sync blocks, and NCCL/compute overlap.

```bash
nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt,cublas,nccl --stats=true --force-overwrite=true -o nsys_run ./runner ...
nsys stats nsys_run.nsys-rep
nsys export --type sqlite --force-overwrite=true -o nsys_run.sqlite nsys_run.nsys-rep
```

Profile a bounded window. Add NVTX around batch, stage, stream, rank, shard, communication, and pipeline phase.

Inspect stream overlap, idle gaps, long CUDA API calls, graph replay/instantiation, NCCL order, host blocking, and log alignment.

# Project Agent Rules

## Operating Rule
- Read `AGENTS.md` before project edits.
- Update `memory/CHANGELOG.md` after meaningful code, config, or architecture changes.
- Update `memory/PROMPTS.md` with user prompts that define requirements.
- Store test outputs, logs, and verification notes under `test_results/`.
- Prefer agent-centered code: explicit contracts, deterministic tests, small files, low hidden state.

## Architecture Source
- Primary architecture contract: `ARCHITECTURE_NEED.md`.
- Current Stream 4 implementation rule: use threshold + compact + CUB/fixed-temp sort/reduce + compact; do not use Stream 4 hash-table dedup.

## Implementation Guardrails
- `State128` logical bytes are `v[0..119]`.
- `State128` padding bytes are `v[120..127]`.
- Persistent frontier padding must be zero.
- `FinalResponse` may temporarily store `target_local_idx` in `v[120..123]`.
- `Hash128` is one logical 128-bit key stored as `{lo, hi}`.
- `CandidateMeta` must remain 32 bytes and 32-byte aligned.
- Stream 3 payload id must be original candidate id, not compact index.
- Stream 4 must not apply shard top-k or semantic shard cap.

# HighloadGpu

Router for CUDA code-writing and high-performance GPU engineering. Default to a single-GPU CUDA hot path first; use multi-GPU or search/decoding guidance only when the task calls for it.

## Pick The Sub-Skill

- CUDA kernels, memory layout, CUTLASS/CUB, graphs, native hot paths: `write-cuda-hot-paths`
- Beam search, top-k/top-p decoding, frontier expansion, candidate selection: `optimize-gpu-search-and-decoding`
- Multi-GPU scaling, rank ownership, peer access, NCCL, overlap: `design-multigpu-systems`
- Python/Rust/C++/CUDA ownership boundaries: `choose-stack-boundaries`
- GPU model, compute capability, CUDA/library docs: `use-nvidia-docs`
- Timeline/stream/NCCL/launch gaps: `use-nsight-systems`
- One-kernel bottleneck: `use-nsight-compute`
- Illegal access/race/init/sync bug: `use-compute-sanitizer`
- Batch/concurrency/shard sweeps: `benchmark-and-sweep-gpu-configs`
- Kaggle/Molab/remote GPU profiling: `profile-remote-gpu-runs`

## Defaults

- Python: wrappers, notebooks, dashboards, CLI/torchrun launch.
- Rust: safe config, validation, artifact/log tooling, host services.
- C++ + CUDA: CPU/GPU hot paths, kernels, CUDA Graphs, NCCL, CUTLASS, CUB/CCCL.

Check current NVIDIA docs before hardware-specific advice. Require correctness checks and profiling evidence before architecture changes.

name: write-cuda-hot-paths
description: Use when writing or optimizing CUDA kernels, memory layouts, and GPU hot paths.
---

# Write CUDA Hot Paths

Primary skill for CUDA code-writing. Hot paths are fixed-capacity, allocation-free, profiler-driven, and explicit about layout, alignment, ownership, and synchronization.

## Workflow

1. State shapes, precision, target GPU, correctness oracle, and measured bottleneck.
2. Choose library vs custom kernel; use custom CUDA where layout, fusion, or control flow makes it worthwhile.
3. Design layout first, implement a small deterministic path, then profile.

## Rules

- Allocate device memory, library temp, NCCL buffers, and graph resources before repeated loops.
- Use explicit capacity guards; fail loudly on overflow.
- Keep CPU readback out of the steady-state path.
- Use CUDA Graphs for repeated launch templates; keep dynamic dispatch on host.
- Add static asserts for cross-kernel metadata size/alignment.
- Store only downstream-needed data; avoid materializing large intermediates when compact keys, indices, or reductions are enough.

## Library Defaults

CUTLASS/cuBLAS for GEMM/tensor-core kernels; CUB/CCCL for sort/reduce/scan/select; NCCL for GPU exchange/collectives; CUDA Runtime/Driver APIs for memory, streams, events, graphs, devices, and peer access.

## Avoid

Dynamic `cudaMalloc`, Python data-plane loops, fine-grained atomics when partition/sort/scan works, custom sort before checking CUB/CCCL, and synchronization that hides ownership bugs.

name: systematic-debugging
description: Use when encountering any bug, test failure, or unexpected behavior, before proposing fixes
---

# Systematic Debugging

## Overview

Random fixes waste time and create new bugs. Quick patches mask underlying issues.

**Core principle:** ALWAYS find root cause before attempting fixes. Symptom fixes are failure.

**Violating the letter of this process is violating the spirit of debugging.**

## The Iron Law

```
NO FIXES WITHOUT ROOT CAUSE INVESTIGATION FIRST
```

If you haven't completed Phase 1, you cannot propose fixes.

## When to Use

Use for ANY technical issue:
- Test failures
- Bugs in production
- Unexpected behavior
- Performance problems
- Build failures
- Integration issues

**Use this ESPECIALLY when:**
- Under time pressure (emergencies make guessing tempting)
- "Just one quick fix" seems obvious
- You've already tried multiple fixes
- Previous fix didn't work
- You don't fully understand the issue

**Don't skip when:**
- Issue seems simple (simple bugs have root causes too)
- You're in a hurry (rushing guarantees rework)
- Manager wants it fixed NOW (systematic is faster than thrashing)

## The Four Phases

You MUST complete each phase before proceeding to the next.

### Phase 1: Root Cause Investigation

**BEFORE attempting ANY fix:**

1. **Read Error Messages Carefully**
   - Don't skip past errors or warnings
   - They often contain the exact solution
   - Read stack traces completely
   - Note line numbers, file paths, error codes

2. **Reproduce Consistently**
   - Can you trigger it reliably?
   - What are the exact steps?
   - Does it happen every time?
   - If not reproducible в†’ gather more data, don't guess

3. **Check Recent Changes**
   - What changed that could cause this?
   - Git diff, recent commits
   - New dependencies, config changes
   - Environmental differen<truncated omitted_approx_tokens="1512" />|
| "Reference too long, I'll adapt the pattern" | Partial understanding guarantees bugs. Read it completely. |
| "I see the problem, let me fix it" | Seeing symptoms в‰  understanding root cause. |
| "One more fix attempt" (after 2+ failures) | 3+ failures = architectural problem. Question pattern, don't fix again. |

## Quick Reference

| Phase | Key Activities | Success Criteria |
|-------|---------------|------------------|
| **1. Root Cause** | Read errors, reproduce, check changes, gather evidence | Understand WHAT and WHY |
| **2. Pattern** | Find working examples, compare | Identify differences |
| **3. Hypothesis** | Form theory, test minimally | Confirmed or new hypothesis |
| **4. Implementation** | Create test, fix, verify | Bug resolved, tests pass |

## When Process Reveals "No Root Cause"

If systematic investigation reveals issue is truly environmental, timing-dependent, or external:

1. You've completed the process
2. Document what you investigated
3. Implement appropriate handling (retry, timeout, error message)
4. Add monitoring/logging for future investigation

**But:** 95% of "no root cause" cases are incomplete investigation.

## Supporting Techniques

These techniques are part of systematic debugging and available in this directory:

- **`root-cause-tracing.md`** - Trace bugs backward through call stack to find original trigger
- **`defense-in-depth.md`** - Add validation at multiple layers after finding root cause
- **`condition-based-waiting.md`** - Replace arbitrary timeouts with condition polling

**Related skills:**
- **superpowers:test-driven-development** - For creating failing test case (Phase 4, Step 1)
- **superpowers:verification-before-completion** - Verify fix worked before claiming success

## Real-World Impact

From debugging sessions:
- Systematic approach: 15-30 minutes to fix
- Random fixes approach: 2-3 hours of thrashing
- First-time fix rate: 95% vs 40%
- New bugs introduced: Near zero vs common

name: use-nsight-systems
description: Use when analyzing GPU timelines.

# Use Nsight Systems

Use Nsight Systems for stream idle gaps, CPU launch/sync blocks, and NCCL/compute overlap.

```bash
nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt,cublas,nccl --stats=true --force-overwrite=true -o nsys_run ./runner ...
nsys stats nsys_run.nsys-rep
nsys export --type sqlite --force-overwrite=true -o nsys_run.sqlite nsys_run.nsys-rep
```

Profile a bounded window. Add NVTX around batch, stage, stream, rank, shard, communication, and pipeline phase.

Inspect stream overlap, idle gaps, long CUDA API calls, graph replay/instantiation, NCCL order, host blocking, and log alignment.

# Use Nsight Compute

Use Nsight Compute after evidence points to one kernel.

```bash
ncu --set full --target-processes all --kernel-name regex:kernel_name --launch-skip 5 --launch-count 10 --force-overwrite -o ncu_kernel ./runner ...
```

Prefer small reproductions. Check critical-path kernel, occupancy limiter, memory throughput/load efficiency, stalls, tensor-core use, and register/shared-memory pressure.

Do not use NCU first for whole-pipeline scheduling; use Nsight Systems.

# Profile Remote GPU Runs

## Routing

Use `work-with-kaggle` or `work-with-molab` for platform operations when available. Use HighloadGpu for architecture/profiling decisions.

## Rules

- Do not leak tokenized session URLs.
- Do not interrupt production/no-timeout runs unless asked.
- Probe `nvidia-smi`, RAM, disk, CUDA Toolkit, compiler, and packages.
- If Nsight is unavailable, use internal timers, NVTX where possible, and structured JSONL logs.
- Keep transient build/checkouts in temp; save final logs/CSVs/PNGs to output and project `test_results/`.
- Verify arch flags from docs/environment.

__global__ void stream1_score_contract_kernel(
    const State128* current_frontier_states,
    const std::uint64_t* parent_base,
    const std::uint32_t* count,
    std::uint32_t* score_ring,
    std::uint32_t ring,
    std::uint32_t ring_slot,
    std::uint32_t ring_slot_count,
    std::uint32_t b_micro) {
    const std::uint32_t candidate = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;
    const std::uint32_t total = b_micro * static_cast<std::uint32_t>(MOVE_COUNT);
    if (candidate >= total) {
        return;
    }
    const std::uint32_t parent_local = candidate / static_cast<std::uint32_t>(MOVE_COUNT);
    const std::uint32_t move = candidate % static_cast<std::uint32_t>(MOVE_COUNT);
    if (parent_local >= count[ring * ring_slot_count + ring_slot]) {
        return;
    }

    const std::uint64_t parent_idx = parent_base[ring * ring_slot_count + ring_slot] + parent_local;
    const State128 state = current_frontier_states[parent_idx];
    std::uint32_t accum = 0;
    for (std::uint32_t p = 0; p < STATE_LEN; ++p) {
        accum += static_cast<std::uint32_t>(state.v[p]) * static_cast<std::uint32_t>((p + 1U) * (move + 1U));
    }
    const std::uint32_t score_key = accum % (SCORE_MAX_KEY + 1U);
    const std::uint64_t offset =
        (((static_cast<std::uint64_t>(ring) * ring_slot_count + ring_slot) * b_micro + parent_local) * MOVE_COUNT) + move;
    score_ring[offset] = score_key;
}

#include "stream_benchmark_common.hpp"

namespace beam::bench {

struct Stream1TransformerBenchmarkResources {
    std::vector<cudaStream_t> streams;
    stream1_weights::ScratchAllocation scratch{};
    std::vector<std::uint64_t*> parent_base;
    std::vector<std::uint32_t*> count;
    std::vector<std::uint32_t*> score;

    Stream1TransformerBenchmarkResources() = default;
    Stream1TransformerBenchmarkResources(const Stream1TransformerBenchmarkResources&) = delete;
    Stream1TransformerBenchmarkResources& operator=(const Stream1TransformerBenchmarkResources&) = delete;

    ~Stream1TransformerBenchmarkResources() {
        cleanup();
    }

    void create_streams_checked(std::uint32_t stream_count) {
        streams.reserve(stream_count);
        for (std::uint32_t i = 0; i < stream_count; ++i) {
            cudaStream_t stream = nullptr;
            BEAM_CUDA_CHECK(cudaStreamCreateWithFlags(&stream, cudaStreamNonBlocking));
            streams.push_back(stream);
        }
    }

    void allocate(
        const Stream1ModelConfig& model,
        std::uint32_t b_micro,
        std::uint32_t concurrent) {
        scratch = stream1_weights::alloc_stream1_scratch(model, b_micro, concurrent);
        parent_base.assign(concurrent, nullptr);
        count.assign(concurrent, nullptr);
        score.assign(concurrent, nullptr);
        for (std::uint32_t i = 0; i < concurrent; ++i) {
            parent_base[i] = device_alloc<std::uint64_t>(1);
            count[i] = device_alloc<std::uint32_t>(1);
            score[i] = device_alloc<std::uint32_t>(static_cast<std::uint64_t>(b_micro) * MOVE_COUNT);
        }
    }

    void cleanup() noexcept {
        cudaDeviceSynchronize();
        for (std::uint64_t* ptr : parent_base) {
            cudaFree(ptr);
        }
        for (std::uint32_t* ptr : count) {
            cudaFree(ptr);
        }

__global__ void stream1_score_contract_kernel(
    const State128* current_frontier_states,
    const std::uint64_t* parent_base,
    const std::uint32_t* count,
    std::uint32_t* score_ring,
    std::uint32_t ring,
    std::uint32_t ring_slot,
    std::uint32_t ring_slot_count,
    std::uint32_t b_micro) {
    const std::uint32_t candidate = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;
    const std::uint32_t total = b_micro * static_cast<std::uint32_t>(MOVE_COUNT);
    if (candidate >= total) {
        return;
    }
    const std::uint32_t parent_local = candidate / static_cast<std::uint32_t>(MOVE_COUNT);
    const std::uint32_t move = candidate % static_cast<std::uint32_t>(MOVE_COUNT);
    if (parent_local >= count[ring * ring_slot_count + ring_slot]) {
        return;
    }

    const std::uint64_t parent_idx = parent_base[ring * ring_slot_count + ring_slot] + parent_local;
    const State128 state = current_frontier_states[parent_idx];
    std::uint32_t accum = 0;
    for (std::uint32_t p = 0; p < STATE_LEN; ++p) {
        accum += static_cast<std::uint32_t>(state.v[p]) * static_cast<std::uint32_t>((p + 1U) * (move + 1U));
    }
    const std::uint32_t score_key = accum % (SCORE_MAX_KEY + 1U);
    const std::uint64_t offset =
        (((static_cast<std::uint64_t>(ring) * ring_slot_count + ring_slot) * b_micro + parent_local) * MOVE_COUNT) + move;
    score_ring[offset] = score_key;
}

#include "stream_benchmark_common.hpp"

namespace beam::bench {

struct Stream1TransformerBenchmarkResources {
    std::vector<cudaStream_t> streams;
    stream1_weights::ScratchAllocation scratch{};
    std::vector<std::uint64_t*> parent_base;
    std::vector<std::uint32_t*> count;
    std::vector<std::uint32_t*> score;

    Stream1TransformerBenchmarkResources() = default;
    Stream1TransformerBenchmarkResources(const Stream1TransformerBenchmarkResources&) = delete;
    Stream1TransformerBenchmarkResources& operator=(const Stream1TransformerBenchmarkResources&) = delete;

    ~Stream1TransformerBenchmarkResources() {
        cleanup();
    }

    void create_streams_checked(std::uint32_t stream_count) {
        streams.reserve(stream_count);
        for (std::uint32_t i = 0; i < stream_count; ++i) {
            cudaStream_t stream = nullptr;
            BEAM_CUDA_CHECK(cudaStreamCreateWithFlags(&stream, cudaStreamNonBlocking));
            streams.push_back(stream);
        }
    }

    void allocate(
        const Stream1ModelConfig& model,
        std::uint32_t b_micro,
        std::uint32_t concurrent) {
        scratch = stream1_weights::alloc_stream1_scratch(model, b_micro, concurrent);
        parent_base.assign(concurrent, nullptr);
        count.assign(concurrent, nullptr);
        score.assign(concurrent, nullptr);
        for (std::uint32_t i = 0; i < concurrent; ++i) {
            parent_base[i] = device_alloc<std::uint64_t>(1);
            count[i] = device_alloc<std::uint32_t>(1);
            score[i] = device_alloc<std::uint32_t>(static_cast<std::uint64_t>(b_micro) * MOVE_COUNT);
        }
    }

    void cleanup() noexcept {
        cudaDeviceSynchronize();
        for (std::uint64_t* ptr : parent_base) {
            cudaFree(ptr);
        }
        for (std::uint32_t* ptr : count) {
            cudaFree(ptr);
        }

# Stream1 Piece-Transformer Kaggle 2xT4 Benchmark v9 QKV Fused - 2026-07-03

## Source

- Kaggle kernel: `trydotatwo/cayley-beam-transformer-2xt4-benchmark`, version 9.
- Branch: `codex/stream1-piece-transformer`.
- Commit: `83c95ea`.
- Hardware: Kaggle `NvidiaTeslaT4`, two Tesla T4 GPUs.
- Backend: native Stream1 piece-transformer fp16 path.
- Change under test: QKV projection fused as CUTLASS GEMM + bias, on top of the previous FF1 GEMM + bias + SiLU fusion.

Downloaded outputs:

- `test_results/kaggle_stream1_transformer_2xt4_v9_qkv_fused_2026-07-03/stream1_transformer_benchmark_rows.csv`
- `test_results/kaggle_stream1_transformer_2xt4_v9_qkv_fused_2026-07-03/cayley-beam-transformer-2xt4-benchmark.log`
- `test_results/kaggle_stream1_transformer_2xt4_v9_qkv_fused_2026-07-03/stream1_transformer_benchmark_reports/`

## Best Points

| version | change | gpu | best b_micro | concurrency | rows/group | ms/group | candidates/s | scratch bytes |
|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 7 | clean tensor attention baseline | 0 | 1024 | 2 | 2048 | 120.4175 | 408179.9 | 655458304 |
| 7 | clean tensor attention baseline | 1 | 1024 | 2 | 2048 | 121.1607 | 405676.1 | 655458304 |
| 8 | FF1 fused | 0 | 512 | 2 | 1024 | 55.0670 | 446292.4 | 327729152 |
| 8 | FF1 fused | 1 | 1024 | 2 | 2048 | 109.5028 | 448865.3 | 655458304 |
| 9 | FF1 + QKV fused | 0 | 1024 | 2 | 2048 | 103.6711 | 474114.7 | 655458304 |
| 9 | FF1 + QKV fused | 1 | 512 | 2 | 1024 | 52.5856 | 467352.5 | 327729152 |

## Interpretation

- v9 vs v8:
  - GPU0: `446292.4 -> 474114.7` candidates/s (`1.062x`).
  - GPU1: `448865.3 -> 467352.5` candidates/s (`1.041x`).
- v9 vs v7 baseline:
  - GPU0: `408179.9 -> 474114.7` candidates/s (`1.162x`).
  - GPU1: `405676.1 -> 467352.5` candidates/s (`1.152x`).
- v9 remains below PyTorch transformer reference:
  - PyTorch direct forward best: `734786.8` candidates/s.
  - PyTorch `batch_process`: `630697.0` candidates/s.
- The QKV bias epilogue is a real improvement, but the remaining gap is still in the transformer attention/layout/remaining epilogues rather than FF1/QKV bias alone.

## Status

- Kaggle log reports branch `codex/stream1-piece-transformer` and commit `83c95ea`.
- Both GPU benchmark reports ended with `status=pass`.
- Bounded grep over the Kaggle log found no traceback/error/failure lines.

__global__ void stream1_transformer_bias_silu_kernel(
    half* __restrict__ matrix,
    const half* __restrict__ bias,
    std::uint32_t rows,
    std::uint32_t cols,
    std::uint32_t dtype) {
    const std::uint32_t i = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;
    const std::uint32_t total = rows * cols;
    if (i >= total) {
        return;
    }
    const std::uint32_t col = i % cols;
    const float x = stream1_transformer_load_scalar_device(matrix, i, dtype) +
        stream1_transformer_load_scalar_device(bias, col, dtype);
    const float y = x / (1.0f + expf(-x));
    stream1_transformer_store_scalar_device(matrix, i, y, dtype);
}

__global__ void stream1_transformer_bias_add_kernel(
    half* __restrict__ matrix,
    const half* __restrict__ bias,
    std::uint32_t rows,
    std::uint32_t cols,
    std::uint32_t dtype) {
    const std::uint32_t i = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;
    const std::uint32_t total = rows * cols;
    if (i >= total) {
        return;
    }
    const std::uint32_t col = i % cols;
    const float x = stream1_transformer_load_scalar_device(matrix, i, dtype) +
        stream1_transformer_load_scalar_device(bias, col, dtype);
    stream1_transformer_store_scalar_device(matrix, i, x, dtype);
}

__global__ void stream1_transformer_bias_silu_kernel(
    half* __restrict__ matrix,
    const half* __restrict__ bias,
    std::uint32_t rows,
    std::uint32_t cols,
    std::uint32_t dtype) {
    const std::uint32_t i = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;
    const std::uint32_t total = rows * cols;
    if (i >= total) {
        return;
    }
    const std::uint32_t col = i % cols;
    const float x = stream1_transformer_load_scalar_device(matrix, i, dtype) +
        stream1_transformer_load_scalar_device(bias, col, dtype);
    const float y = x / (1.0f + expf(-x));
    stream1_transformer_store_scalar_device(matrix, i, y, dtype);
}

__global__ void stream1_transformer_bias_add_kernel(
    half* __restrict__ matrix,
    const half* __restrict__ bias,
    std::uint32_t rows,
    std::uint32_t cols,
    std::uint32_t dtype) {
    const std::uint32_t i = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;
    const std::uint32_t total = rows * cols;
    if (i >= total) {
        return;
    }
    const std::uint32_t col = i % cols;
    const float x = stream1_transformer_load_scalar_device(matrix, i, dtype) +
        stream1_transformer_load_scalar_device(bias, col, dtype);
    stream1_transformer_store_scalar_device(matrix, i, x, dtype);
}

inline std::vector<State128> make_state_batch(
    State128 seed,
    std::uint32_t count,
    std::uint32_t num_classes) {
    std::vector<State128> states(count, seed);
    for (std::uint32_t i = 0; i < count; ++i) {
        states[i].v[0] = static_cast<std::uint8_t>((states[i].v[0] + i) % num_classes);
        states[i].v[STATE_LEN] = 0;
    }
    return states;
}

inline std::vector<State128> make_state_batch(
    State128 seed,
    std::uint32_t count,
    std::uint32_t num_classes) {
    std::vector<State128> states(count, seed);
    for (std::uint32_t i = 0; i < count; ++i) {
        states[i].v[0] = static_cast<std::uint8_t>((states[i].v[0] + i) % num_classes);
        states[i].v[STATE_LEN] = 0;
    }
    return states;
}

# Stream1 Transformer Graph Benchmark Mode 2026-07-03

## Change

- Added `BEAM_STREAM1_TRANSFORMER_GRAPH_BENCH=1` to `tools/stream_benchmark_transformer.cu`.
- In graph mode the benchmark captures one `stream1_transformer_inference_cuda` graph per stream, instantiates it, and times repeated `cudaGraphLaunch` calls.
- This is benchmark-only instrumentation. It does not change `cuda/stream1.cu`, the MLP path, dispatcher semantics, or production solver kernels.

## Why

The non-graph microbenchmark times the host enqueue path between CUDA events. That is useful for raw launch overhead, but the solver/dispatcher uses CUDA graph replay for repeated Stream1 work. Graph timing is the closer performance gate for comparing production Stream1 transformer changes.

## Verification

Environment:

# Stream1 Transformer Graph Benchmark Mode 2026-07-03

## Change

- Added `BEAM_STREAM1_TRANSFORMER_GRAPH_BENCH=1` to `tools/stream_benchmark_transformer.cu`.
- In graph mode the benchmark captures one `stream1_transformer_inference_cuda` graph per stream, instantiates it, and times repeated `cudaGraphLaunch` calls.
- This is benchmark-only instrumentation. It does not change `cuda/stream1.cu`, the MLP path, dispatcher semantics, or production solver kernels.

## Why

The non-graph microbenchmark times the host enqueue path between CUDA events. That is useful for raw launch overhead, but the solver/dispatcher uses CUDA graph replay for repeated Stream1 work. Graph timing is the closer performance gate for comparing production Stream1 transformer changes.

## Verification

Environment:

```text
Docker image: gpu-dev-cutlass-nsight:cuda128-sm120
Workspace: D:\100XH100\.worktrees\stream1-piece-transformer
Weights: test_results/kaggle_stream1_transformer_2xt4_v9_qkv_fused_2026-07-03/stream1_transformer_weights_fp16
```

Commands:

```bash
cmake --build build-stream1-opt --target stream1_transformer_cuda_tests dispatcher_cuda_tests stream_benchmark -j2
./build-stream1-opt/stream1_transformer_cuda_tests
./build-stream1-opt/dispatcher_cuda_tests
cmake --build build-stream1-opt --target contract_tests -j2
./build-stream1-opt/contract_tests
BEAM_WEIGHT_DIR=test_results/kaggle_stream1_transformer_2xt4_v9_qkv_fused_2026-07-03/stream1_transformer_weights_fp16 \
BEAM_STREAM_BENCH_REPORT=test_results/stream1_transformer_graphbench_verify_1024x2_2026-07-03.md \
BEAM_STREAM1_TRANSFORMER_GRAPH_BENCH=1 \
BEAM_STREAM1_TRANSFORMER_B_MICRO=1024 \
BEAM_STREAM1_TRANSFORMER_CONCURRENCY=2 \
./build-stream1-opt/stream_benchmark 991
```

Results:

```text
stream1_transformer_cuda_tests=pass
dispatcher_cuda_tests=pass
contract_tests=pass
stream1_transformer_micro b_micro=1024 concurrency=2 rows_per_launch_group=2048 ms_per_launch_group=84.3790 parents_per_sec=24271.5 candidates_per_sec=582514.8 scratch_bytes=655458304
```

## Notes

- Earlier local experiments with SM75 FMHA, cuBLASLt QKV/FF1, and QKV tile changes were not kept because they were slower or not yet proven under graph replay.
- Local RTX measurements are still not a final T4/A100 gate. The next required check is Kaggle 2xT4 graph replay using the same benchmark mode.
